title: Safety & Policy
summary:
**Product:** any model deployment that must follow safety, privacy and authorization rules under normal, borderline and adversarial use. Two sides must be measured together: **violations** (it did something it must not) and **over-refusal** (it refused something it should help with). Lowering one by raising the other is not progress.

**What to measure**
- **Harm and policy violation rate** on clearly disallowed requests, weighted by severity.
- **Over-refusal rate** on benign and borderline requests; **safe completion** (a helpful partial answer within limits).
- **Privacy and data exfiltration**: PII, secrets, system prompt, cross-user data.
- **Authorization**: no high-risk external action without permission.
- **Prompt injection** success rate via user text, files, web pages, tool outputs.
- **Consistency** across paraphrase, languages, encodings and multi-turn pressure.

**How to measure:** labelled prompt sets with graders (rules for objective leaks, judges for fuzzy policy, humans for uncertain cases) plus **red-teaming**. Keep a **holdout** set separate from attack templates you tuned against.

**Failure modes:** overfitting to known jailbreaks, refusal inflation, policy gaps in other languages, regressions after a system-prompt edit, one severe incident hidden in a good average.

**Choosing metrics:** set hard gates per severe category (rate with confidence bound, not a lone average), report violation and over-refusal side by side, send judge-uncertain cases to humans, and rerun the full critical suite after every policy or prompt change. See [tool-using agents](#/sd/f/eval-tool-agent) for authorization checks and [conversational assistants](#/sd/f/eval-conversational) for judge calibration.

drills.q: A model is tested on 500 clearly harmful prompts and 500 benign-but-borderline prompts. It complies with 15 of the harmful ones and refuses 60 of the benign ones. What is the over-refusal rate on the benign set, in percent?
drills.explain: 60 / 500 = 12%. The violation rate is 15/500 = 3%. A policy change that cut violations by refusing more would hide a regression in usefulness unless both are reported.

drills.q: You test a model on n independent harmful prompts and observe zero violations. Using the rule of three (95% upper confidence bound on the rate ≈ 3/n), about how many prompts do you need to claim the true violation rate is below 0.5%?
drills.explain: 3 / n <= 0.005 gives n >= 600. 'Zero failures in 50 tests' only supports a bound near 6%, so severe-category gates need large, fresh test sets.

drills.q: Your safety score improves from 97% to 99% after tightening the system prompt. Which additional result must you check before shipping?
options: Over-refusal and helpfulness on benign and borderline requests, because the improvement may come from refusing more
drills.explain: A model that refuses everything has a perfect safety score. Report violation and over-refusal on matched sets and look at the trade-off.

drills.q: The team tunes defences against a library of 200 known jailbreak templates and reports a 1% attack success rate on that library. What is the main evaluation weakness?
options: The result is measured on the same data used to tune, so it overfits; keep a holdout of unseen attacks and keep adding fresh red-team material
Attack success rate cannot be measured
1% is too low to be real
drills.explain: Defences that memorise templates fail on paraphrases and new strategies. A held-out, regularly refreshed attack set measures generalization.

drills.q: In a month of evaluation, 9,990 of 10,000 prompts were handled correctly, but one response leaked another user's account number. Reported average safety: 99.9%. What is the right release treatment?
options: Treat the leak as a separate severe-category failure with its own zero-tolerance gate, investigate the root cause, and rerun the critical suite
Count it only if two reviewers saw it
drills.explain: Averages hide rare, severe incidents. Privacy and authorization failures need independent gates and individual incident review.

drills.q: Put the release process after a system-prompt or policy change in order.
items: Rerun the full critical safety suite, including a fresh holdout set
Compare violation and over-refusal per category and slice with the previous version
Send judge-uncertain samples to human review
Apply the hard gates for severe categories (pass or block)
Ship and monitor refusals, appeals and reports
drills.explain: Policy and prompt edits can regress unrelated categories, so the whole critical suite reruns. Uncertain judge verdicts should reach humans, not be forced into pass or fail.
